title: Classical & operant conditioning
examples: Can you explain the difference between classical and operant conditioning?
How does Skinner's work relate to behavior modification?
What is the difference between positive and negative reinforcement?

explain.say: Today we will explore how learning happens in psychology. We will look at two main types of learning. First we will study classical conditioning from Ivan Pavlov.
In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a natural one. For example, the sound of a bell predicts food arriving. Eventually, the bell alone makes the dog salivate.
Next we look at operant conditioning, developed by B.F. Skinner. This focuses on consequences shaping behaviour. The organism learns through rewards and punishments.
Reinforcement increases a behaviour's likelihood. Positive reinforcement adds something good, like praise. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, like a buzzing sound.
Skinner also described reinforcement schedules. Continuous reinforcement works best initially. However, intermittent reinforcement makes behaviour very resistant to extinction.
Imagine you are learning to ride a bicycle. Initially, you need constant support, which is continuous reinforcement. As you improve, you only need occasional reminders to keep balancing.

draw.text: Bicycle: Needs less support over time

faq.q: What is the core difference between Pavlov and Skinner's theories?
faq.a: Pavlov focused on involuntary biological responses to stimuli. Skinner focused on how voluntary actions are shaped by their consequences.

faq.q: Is negative reinforcement always bad for a person?
faq.a: No, it is simply the removal of something a person dislikes. For example, taking aspirin removes the unpleasant headache.

faq.q: What is extinction in classical conditioning?
faq.a: Extinction happens when the conditioned stimulus is presented repeatedly without the unconditioned stimulus. The response will gradually disappear.
asks: What happens if I keep ringing the bell without food?
How do you stop a learned response?

faq.q: Why is the variable ratio schedule so powerful?
faq.a: Because the reward is unpredictable, the behaviour is highly motivated to continue. This is why gambling is so addictive.
asks: Why do slot machines work so well?

faq.q: Does operant conditioning apply to emotions?
faq.a: While emotions are complex, the response to emotional triggers can be shaped by operant principles. We learn what actions lead to positive feelings.
asks: Is emotion just a learned behaviour?

facts: Classical conditioning involves pairing a neutral stimulus with an unconditioned stimulus.
Operant conditioning suggests that behaviour is controlled by its consequences.
Positive reinforcement involves adding a desirable stimulus to increase behaviour.
Intermittent reinforcement schedules lead to the most persistent behaviours.

quiz.say: If a student studies hard and receives high marks, this is an example of:
quiz.why: High marks are desirable, and receiving them increases the likelihood that the student will study hard again.

wrong.1: This would involve removing something unpleasant, not adding a mark.
wrong.2: This theory requires pairing two distinct stimuli together.
wrong.3: This schedule relates to unpredictable rewards, not consistent academic success.

quiz.say: A dog salivates at the sound of a specific chime, even when no food is present. This learned association is best described as:
quiz.why: The salivation in response to the chime alone is the learned response after conditioning has occurred.

wrong.0: The unconditioned response is the natural reaction to food, not the chime.
wrong.1: This is a response, not the addition of a reward.
wrong.2: This process involves the removal of an unpleasant stimulus.
